s.d: (formal) Of, characterized by, or relating to abusive or harsh criticism.
x: Faced with a vituperate Serbian nationalism and the despotic actions of Slobodan Milošević, who took power in the late 1980s, Slovenia and Croatia seceded from federal Yugoslavia in June 1991[…].

s.d: (formal, rare) Which has been abusively or harshly criticized; also, deserving harsh criticism.

vituperation.e: From Latin vituperātiō (“censure, blame”), equivalent to vituperate + -ion.

s.d: abusive or venomous language used to express blame or censure or bitter deep-seated ill will
(uncountable) The act of vituperating; severely blaming or censuring.
(uncountable) Criticism or invective that is sustained and overly harsh; abuse, severe blame or censure.
x: "Do you call me a spy?" / "And what have you called me? Because you are a husband, is the privilege of vituperation to be all on your side?"

His face turned red with passion; he made one bound, hurled me across the house with a sweep of his arm, spun the wheel down, and began to pour out a stream of vituperation upon me which lasted till he was out of breath.

vituperative.e: Formed from vituperātus, perfect passive participle of Latin vituperō (“to blame, to censure”) + -ive; by surface analysis, vituperate + -ive.

s.d: marked by harshly abusive criticism
x: his scathing remarks about silly lady novelists
her vituperative railing

s.d: Marked by harsh abuse; abusive, often with ranting or railing.
x: Floris gave the play a vituperative review laced with frequent personal insults.
[…] ten times in a day calling the child of his prayers TRISTRAM!—Melancholy dissyllable of sound! which, to his ears, was unison to Nincompoop, and every name vituperative under heaven.

viva.e: Borrowed from Spanish viva and Italian viva.

s.d: an examination conducted by spoken communication
A shout of applause.
x: When the cibolero returned to the plain, he was received with a fresh burst of vivas, and kerchiefs were waved to greet him.

s.d: An oral examination, typically for an academic qualification.
(dated) To cheer, applaud
x: ...the people clapped and vivaed, groaned and hooted, as they were pleased or disappointed, until at length the intense excitement began to subside...
The next evening Paine went to the theatre. The state-box had been prepared for him. The house rose and vivaed as he entered.

s.d: To subject to an examination of this kind.
x: I was vivaed by Charles Cannan, who was then a Fellow of Trinity...
Throughout his life, he took college responsibilities seriously, he came to All Souls whenever possible on weekends, he vivaed or interviewed candidates...

s.d: Long live ... ! (used to express acclaim or support).
x: The message has been mostly perverted from the moment of his death, but it hasn't been invalidated. So, viva Jesus of Nazareth and joy to the world!

viva voce.e: From Latin vīvā (“living”) and vōce (“voice”) (ablative of vōx).

(of tempo) very fast and lively

lively, in music

s.d: vigorous and animated
x: a vibrant group that challenged the system
a charming and vivacious hostess

s.d: Lively and animated; full of life and energy.
x: Given the vivacious young redhead's attractiveness, some might have assumed he had more than simply professional reasons for sheepdogging her career, but they would have been wrong. He'd seen something in her ...

s.d: (obsolete) Long-lived.
(rare) Difficult to kill.

the activity of giving vitality and vigour to something

x: She seemed molded from fire and air, and vivified at some Voltaic pile of August thunder-clouds heaped against the sunset.
Persephone, the life force which vivifies all in the spring time, producing the manifold harvests of earth, descends with Plouton to the under world in autumn.

s.d: To impart vitality to.

s.d: producing living young (not eggs)
Being born alive, as are most mammals, some reptiles, and a few fish (as opposed to being laid as an egg and subsequently hatching, as do all birds and many other species).

an eelpout of northern Europe that is viviparous

cut (a body) open while still alive
x: people no longer vivisect animals — it's considered unethical

(uncountable) The act or instance of cutting, surgery, or other invasive treatment of a living organism for the purposes of physiological or pathological scientific investigation.

s.d: a malicious woman with a fierce temper
a female fox
A malicious, quarrelsome or temperamental woman.
x: He was prudent and industrious, and so good a husbandman, that he might have led a very easy and comfortable life, had not an arrant vixen of a wife soured his domestic quiet.
(Mimic): 'I used the plans to build a Steam Engine of my own. I was almost done when that vixen swiped it!'

s.d: (colloquial) A racy or salacious woman who is sexually attractive; any attractive woman.
(colloquial) A wife who has sex with other men with her husband's consent.

viz..e:
From Medieval Latin viꝫ, from Latin vidēlicet (“that is to say, namely”), short for vidēre licet (“it is permitted to see”, literally “to-look (it) allows”). The ‘z’ comes from the similarity between ꝫ (‘et’) and the cursive form of the letter z, with the former having originated as a common abbreviation (specifically, a Tironian note), used by Latin scribes in the Middle Ages, for the suffix -et (among others).
Compare ⁊ (‘et’), the Tironian symbol for the Latin word et (“and”) and for its equi

s.d: as follows
Videlicet: namely, to wit, that is to say, specifically, as an illustration.
x: I am at this period, viz. in 1812, living in a cottage; […]
The fact is, when Captain Dobbin blushed so, and looked so, it was necessary to inform the young ladies, viz., that he had been calling at Mr. Sedley's house already, […]

vizier.e: From Ottoman Turkish وزیر (vezir) (Turkish vezir) (via French vizir), from Arabic وَزِير (wazīr, “helper, aide, minister”, literally “one who bears (the burden of office)”). Doublet of wazir.

s.d: a high official in a Muslim government (especially in the Ottoman Empire)
The highest-ranking official or minister in ancient Egypt or Ebla; a chief administrator or a chancellor.
An ancient Mesopotamian civil servant, the sukkal (𒈛 (sukkal)).
x: As Inanna prepares to descend she fastens the seven divine laws to her side, and as she walks toward the netherworld she speaks to her vizier, Ninshubur.
Momus is not otherwise attested as Zeus’s advisor, but in name and function he matches Apsu’s vizier Mummu.

the position of vizier
